title.say: Thirty-six letters. One sound for each.

title: This is the story of the Albanian alphabet, and of the first book every child opens.
early: Albanian was spoken long before it was written down.
The oldest dated line we have is a baptism formula from fourteen sixty-two.
The first known printed book followed in fifteen fifty-five.

scripts.say: But for centuries, there was no single alphabet.

scripts: In the north, people wrote with Latin letters. In the south, with Greek ones. Others used Arabic script.
And some invented alphabets of their own.
primer: In eighteen forty-four, one of those inventors printed the first Albanian primer, the ahbeh tahreh.
More primers followed, in different alphabets and in both dialects.
By the start of the twentieth century, at least six alphabets were in use.
congress: In November nineteen oh eight, fifty delegates met in Mahnasteer, today's Beetola.

congress.say: They had one question to settle. Which letters?

congress: A commission of eleven chose a Latin alphabet, alongside the older Istanbul one.
Within a few years, only the Latin one was still in use.
letters: It has thirty-six letters: seven vowels and twenty-nine consonants.
Nine of them are written as pairs.
today: In nineteen seventy-two, a congress in Teerahna agreed on one standard spelling.
In twenty twelve, Albania and Kosovo presented a shared ahbeh tahreh, and a new joint edition followed in twenty twenty-two.
Even the old invented scripts now have a place in Unicode, the standard behind every screen.
outro: This weekend, Albanians marked one hundred and eighteen years since that decision.

outro.say: And every autumn, new first-graders open the ahbeh tahreh, and meet the same thirty-six letters.
